outputs.L1:
The dim sea glints chill. The white sun is shy,  
And the skeleton weeds and the never-dry,  
Rough, long grasses keep white with frost  
At the hilltop by the finger-post;  
The smoke of the traveller’s-joy is puffed  
Over hawthorn berry and hazel tuft.

I read the sign. Which way shall I go?  
A voice says, “You would not have doubted so  
At twenty.” Another voice, gentle with scorn,  
Says, “At twenty you wished you had never been born.”

One hazel lost a leaf of gold  
From a tuft at the tip, when the first voice told  
The other he wished to know what ’twould be  
To be sixty by this same post. “You shall see,”  
He laughed—and I had to join his laughter—  
“You shall see; but either before or after,  
Whatever happens, it must befall,  
A mouthful of earth to remedy all  
Regrets and wishes shall freely be given;  
And if there be a flaw in that heaven,  
’Twill be freedom to wish, and your wish may be  
To be here or anywhere, talking to me,  
No matter what the weather, on earth,  
At any age between death and birth,  
To see what day or night can be,  
The sun and the frost, the land and the sea,  
Summer, Autumn, Winter, Spring—  
With a poor man of any sort, down to a king,  
Standing upright out in the air,  
Wondering where he shall journey—O where?”
outputs.L2:
The darkened sea gleams coldly beneath a pale, reluctant sun. On the hill beside the signpost, bare weeds and coarse, enduring grasses are whitened by frost. Wisps from the traveller’s-joy drift like smoke across red hawthorn berries and clumps of hazel.

I study the directions and wonder which road to take. One voice tells me that, at twenty, I would not have hesitated like this. A second voice, softly mocking, replies that when I was twenty, I regretted ever having been born.

A golden leaf fell from the end of a hazel spray as the first voice admitted to the other that he wanted to know what it would feel like to stand at this same post at sixty.

“You will find out,” the other answered with a laugh, and I could not help laughing too. “You will find out—but sooner or later, whatever else may occur, a mouthful of soil will come to cure every longing and regret. It will be granted without cost. And if that heaven has any defect, perhaps it will be the liberty to go on wishing. Then your desire might be to return here—or to be anywhere at all—speaking with me on earth, regardless of the weather, at any age between birth and death.

“You may wish to witness everything that day and night can offer: sunlight and frost, earth and ocean, summer, autumn, winter, and spring. And there may stand beneath the open sky any man, from the poorest person to a king, upright and uncertain, asking himself which road he should follow—and where, indeed, he ought to go.”
outputs.L3:
At the top of a frost-covered hill, a traveler pauses beside a signpost, unsure which path to follow. The wintry landscape reflects the traveler’s uncertainty, turning the moment into more than a simple choice of direction: it becomes a meditation on the course of an entire life.

As the traveler hesitates, competing inner voices recall the emotions of youth—self-doubt, despair, and curiosity about what it will mean to grow old. These voices suggest that uncertainty is not confined to the present moment but has accompanied the traveler throughout life. One voice offers a stark consolation, observing that death will eventually bring an end to every regret, longing, and unfulfilled wish.

Yet the poem also imagines a more hopeful possibility. Heaven is presented as the freedom to revisit any earthly moment: any place, season, experience, or stage of life. In this vision, eternity allows a person to return to what was loved, lost, or left behind.

The traveler’s dilemma therefore represents a universal human journey. Whether someone is poor and powerless or wealthy and royal, everyone eventually reaches moments of uncertainty and asks the same fundamental question: where should I go next?
outputs.L4:
At a frosty crossroads, an aging traveler stopped to consider the paths before him. Snow lay thinly over the ground, whitening the stones and stiffening the grass, while the bare branches above him shivered in the wind. One road descended toward a valley where smoke rose from distant chimneys. Another climbed into dark woods. A third curved out of sight beneath a pale winter sky. He had traveled far, yet he still could not tell which way promised peace.

As he stood there, he imagined his younger self beside him: impatient, bright-eyed, and certain that every choice must lead to greatness.

“Why do you hesitate?” the young man asked. “Take the steep road. It may be difficult, but something wonderful must lie beyond the hill.”

The older traveler smiled. “You always believed difficulty guaranteed reward.”

“And you always feared losing what you already had.”

“That is because I learned how easily things are lost.”

The young man looked down each road in turn. “Then choose the valley. There will be warmth, companionship, and shelter.”

“There may also be obligations I no longer have the strength to bear.”

“Then take the road through the woods.”

“And wander alone?”

“You used to long for solitude.”

“I did, until I had enough of it.”

The younger self laughed. “Age has made you impossible to satisfy.”

“No,” the traveler replied. “Age has taught me that every path contains both gain and loss. Whatever road I choose, I will sometimes wish I had chosen another.”

For a moment, neither spoke. Snow began to fall, lightly at first, each flake turning in the air before settling on the traveler’s cloak.

The old man remembered other crossroads: spring mornings when the world had seemed newly made; summer afternoons filled with ambition and desire; autumn evenings when he counted what he had gathered and what had slipped away. At every age he had believed that certainty waited just beyond the next decision. Yet each answer had created new questions, and each fulfilled wish had given birth to another.

“Do you regret the road we took?” his younger self asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Do you regret the roads we left behind?”

“Sometimes.”

“Then what wisdom have all these years given you?”

The traveler considered this. “Only that regret is not proof that one chose wrongly. It is the shadow cast by every choice. To choose one life is to surrender countless others.”

The young man frowned. “That is a bleak lesson.”

“Not entirely. There will come a day when I no longer remember these roads. Death will silence regret, but it will also silence longing. It will end disappointment, but it will end wonder too. No desire will trouble me then, because there will be no tomorrow in which desire might be fulfilled.”

The snow thickened, softening the outlines of the three roads until they seemed less separate than before.

“So what should we do?” the young man asked.

“We should choose while choosing is still possible.”

“Even without knowing where the road leads?”

“No one has ever known.”

The traveler turned toward the climbing path. Perhaps it would exhaust him. Perhaps the woods would be lonely, and perhaps he would look back before nightfall and wish he had gone down to the welcoming lights of the valley. But the cold air still entered his lungs, his heart still answered it, and the world—winter-bound though it was—had not finished changing.

He took his first step. Beside him, his younger self vanished, though something of the youth’s eagerness remained in his stride.

Spring would come again, whether he saw it or not. Summer would ripen, autumn would fade, and winter would return. Life repeated its seasons, but no season was ever quite the same, and no traveler met it at the same age twice. That was why each uncertain step mattered. Regret and desire belonged not merely to youth or age, but to being alive.

The traveler continued up the road as snow covered the crossroads behind him.
outputs.L5: The road was rough, and the journey was long. Yet with every difficult step, the travelers grew stronger. By the time they reached the summit, they understood that the rough path had made the view even more meaningful.

### “The Sign-Post”  
*Edward Thomas*

The dim sea glints chill. The white sun is shy.  
And the skeleton weeds and the never-dry,  
Rough, long grasses keep white with frost  
At the hill-top by the finger-post;  
The smoke of the traveller’s-joy is puffed  
Over hawthorn berry and hazel tuft.  

I read the sign. Which way shall I go?  
A voice says: You would not have doubted so  
At twenty. Another voice gentle with scorn  
Says: At twenty you wished you had never been born.  

One hazel lost a leaf of gold  
From a tuft at the tip, when the first voice told  
The other he wished to know what ’twould be  
To be sixty by this same post. “You shall see,”  
He laughed—and I had to join his laughter—  
“You shall see; but either before or after,  
Whatever happens, it must befall,  
A mouthful of earth to remedy all  
Regrets and wishes shall freely be given;  
And if there be a flaw in that heaven  
’Twill be freedom to wish, and your wish may be  
To be here or anywhere.”
